content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics

Hi, I'm Kristina Smekens. Thanks for joining me for the TEACH writing PD mini-series. In this episode, we'll revisit the concept of building a class writing rubric—which was first introduced in Ep 4. Then I'll reveal how to raise the writing expectations throughout the year while respecting the diverse range of writing abilities in your classroom.

In the primary grades, writing rubrics are often viewed as an assessment tool meant only for teachers, as their typically word-heavy format seems to be challenging for young students to understand. However, in Episode 4, we learned how to create a simplified writing rubric WITH students that they can both read and use effectively.

This initial writing rubric can be introduced at any point during the year, but the earlier, the better. In Episode 4, I explained that this rubric has 3-5 levels, with Level 1 reflecting the characteristics of your lowest writers and the highest level extending just beyond what your strongest writers can do independently. It's important to have a tool that honors EVERY student in the class, from the advanced to the emerging.

Each level of an initial kid-friendly rubric includes 2 pieces of information: a writing sample that visually depicts what that level looks and sounds like, and clear, simple criteria that describe how the levels differ from one another.

Ep 4 emphasized the value of introducing this yearlong writing tool to primary students in order to: define what "good" writing is, show them how to recognize what may be missing in their own writing, and provide them with concrete next steps to correct or improve it.

section_name: WHERE Do You Add a New Level
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — WHERE Do You Add a New Level

Regardless of when you start your Class Writing rubric, it will eventually need to evolve. And that brings us to the focus of this video: the logistics of WHERE, WHEN, WHAT, and HOW to update an instructional writing rubric used within primary classrooms.

WHERE do you add a new level? The rubric will be a permanent resource in the classroom environment. This is not a temporary piece of chart paper, but a growing assessment tool students will reference all year long.

To accommodate the growth of your rubric, you'll need a large section of wall space, ideally placed low on the wall. The rubric is designed this way so all students can easily walk up to it, interact with its criteria, and compare it with their own writing. A common choice of many teachers is to display their classroom writing rubric below the whiteboard, as it provides long horizontal space in reach of young students.

As a primary writing rubric evolves, the new levels are added TO THE RIGHT. This mimics the direction of reading text and symbolizes progression. Likewise, writers advance in their writing development by moving to the right on a rubric. This growing visual reflects the increasing expectations of writing and students' progress in achieving them.

section_name: WHAT Do You Add in a New Level
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — WHAT Do You Add in a New Level

For each new level, you will provide both the updated criteria and a corresponding writing sample. Depending on the skills outlined within the initial rubric, these increased levels will likely reference some of the following skills: additional details WITHIN the picture, additional labels AROUND the picture, a complete thought written BELOW the picture, correct spelling of WWW (high-frequency words), sound stretch spelling of big words, sentence capitals, sentence end marks, multiple sentences, a title, a beginning, an ending, and transition words.

Take note that a writing rubric is NOT solely focused on language foundations. While concepts of print ARE a significant part of any primary writing rubric, it's equally important to nurture students' ability to express and develop their own ideas. Your state writing standards require instruction in BOTH the growth of sentence-level skills AND the development and organization of ideas—regardless if the student produces multiple sentences or communicates primarily through a picture.

AFTER a writing skill has been taught, modeled, and practiced, THEN we can hold students accountable for it within the rubric.

section_name: Parallel Criteria and Preparing New Levels
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — Parallel Criteria and Preparing New Levels

When it's time to up the ante of the class writing rubric, we will need to present it using parallel criteria. This term was first defined in Ep 4 as a characteristic describing how the skills are referenced AMONG the rubric levels. Once a skill is added to the rubric, it needs to be addressed and represented in all of the remaining levels. This creates a parallel set of expectations. Rubrics describe the same bulleted ingredients—just at increasing degrees of quality.

Consequently, any new level must reference skills from the previous level—and identify additional expectations.

After determining the criteria for this new level, revise it to be simple in language and minimal in words. Consider drawing small visuals or writer tools to aid early readers in its comprehension.

You will ALSO need to create a new writing sample that represents these new expectations. This will provide a concrete example of what THAT level looks like. Be sure to create this sample on the same topic used when building the initial rubric. This is to be a topic that students can relate to but not one that they would likely write about independently.

One key advantage of an instructional rubric is that it keeps previously taught skills in front of students. This combats the many students who tend to demonstrate a skill in their writing UNTIL they learn something new. As their writer concentration shifts, the first skill often falls off their radars. But a GROWING rubric includes the foundational criteria while UPPING the ante with new skills that have been taught and practiced.

This reinforces that an instructional rubric isn't CHANGING in its expectations—it's GROWING them. It doesn't shift its focus but broadens the range of skills it holds students accountable for. This cumulative approach increases the rigor and demonstrates the mantra of all instructional rubrics—Teach more. Expect more.

section_name: HOW Do You Reveal a New Level
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — HOW Do You Reveal a New Level

With the prep work complete, it's time to introduce this new rubric level to your students.

A rubric update might begin with students sitting near the CURRENT rubric posted on the wall. Starting at Level 1, quickly reread the familiar criteria aloud while highlighting the skills in the sample. Focus on the positive aspects and what is evident in the writing—without mentioning what's missing.

Move to the next level, reminding students that rubrics show us how to make our own writing EVEN BETTER. Then, read the criteria for THAT level, noting the new, color-coded expectations and their application in the corresponding writing sample.

Repeat this process for all current rubric levels. Then remind students that the initial class rubric was created earlier in the year. And at that time, you told them it was done... for now. Announce that students have learned new writing skills that need to be added to the rubric—and today is the day!

Reveal the newest level and criteria that you prepared ahead of time and post it to the right of the previous version. Highlight the skills that carry over from the previous level. These might appear in black or be listed lower to emphasize that these are already familiar to the students. Announce that there are also new skills writers are expected to include at this level. Point to the new additions listed at the top of the criteria, and read them aloud while connecting each to your previous mini-lessons. Share the corresponding writing sample and identify evidence of the new expectations in action.

Throughout this lesson, emphasize that writers start in different places and grow at different paces—but they all share the same goal: to move up to the next level. Make it clear that this newest level is NOT an expectation for everyone TODAY but rather a target for growth. The goal is steady improvement. We want everyone to move to the next level, and then the next. This reinforces that writers will rarely skip over entire levels; they move THROUGH them.

Consequently, always deliver rubric-update lessons in a way that honors where each student currently is, while encouraging him to reach for the next level. This helps prevent students at the lower end of the rubric from feeling overwhelmed by unrealistic expectations, while ensuring that advanced writers continue to be challenged.

section_name: Student Use of the Rubric and X-Ray Editing
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — Student Use of the Rubric and X-Ray Editing

Within this same lesson, reiterate how students are to use the rubric during writing time. (This was described in detail within Ep 4 of this mini series.) With your writing in hand, walk up to the posted rubric. Determine which writing sample LOOKS most like yours. Put your finger on the first skill in its criteria. Look for that skill done accurately within your own writing. If you discover the skill is missing or wrong, remind students this is when they would go back to their seats to add or fix it. Continue modeling this process for each skill listed in the criteria for THAT level.

Then explain they STILL aren't done. Model how to look to the right, to look UP the rubric at the next level. Point out that the new RED skills listed guide the writer as to what to do next in order to earn THAT star.

By consistently updating the rubric WHILE honoring each student's current level, we create an environment where all students can progress at their own pace. They all have a clear roadmap for improvement with achievable next steps. They all have a tool that supports individual development. And they all have realistic expectations that stretch their abilities—without overwhelming them.

Every time you update the rubric, prepare the criteria and writing sample beforehand. Then, hold a class meeting in LIEU of that day's whole-class writing mini-lesson. While you won't be targeting a new grade-level writing skill that day, you WILL be delivering valuable instruction that nurtures continuous growth in your young writers.

As I first mentioned in Episode 4, student involvement in the building of the class writing rubric is crucial. AND this involvement should continue each time the rubric is updated. By doing so, students have the opportunity to witness the gradual increase in expectations, making them more familiar with each incremental change. They are present as new criteria are added, watching the rubric grow and becoming more comfortable with its evolving expectations. The more students participate in developing the rubric, the better they understand its expectations and the more quickly they can integrate them into their own writing.

Now, let me alert you to a potential problem that comes with increased rubric expectations: While some students CAN achieve a higher level, there will be days that they don't WANT to. As the list of criteria gets longer and longer, they find themselves having to assess for more and more criteria. Consequently, we need to MOTIVATE them to WANT to use the rubric. One strategy is to introduce a set of plastic glasses as a fun writer tool. Pop the lenses out of colorful sunglasses and teach students how to execute x-ray editing.

Assign a particular pair of glasses—and a coordinating pen color—to each skill on the rubric criteria. If the criteria indicates red means they should check their writing for end marks, then they read their entire piece for application of end marks only. As they confirm EACH end mark is accurate, they trace over it with the red pen. And if they find a mistake or missing punctuation, they add it in with the red pen. As they prepare to self-assess their writing for the next skill, say sentence capitals, they will switch their glasses and pen color.

section_name: WHEN Do You Add a New Level and Naming Levels
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — WHEN Do You Add a New Level and Naming Levels

Since we can't predict precisely WHEN you will add a level to your class rubric or HOW MANY levels you will have by the end of the year, it's important to name your levels in a limitless manner. The most common approach is to use a star system. But there ARE other techniques. Check out this growing caterpillar created by a kindergarten teacher in Illinois. A new section of the caterpillar's body was added to represent each new level. As the school year was ending and the teacher knew it was her last rubric-update lesson, she posted the final criteria and writing sample on a butterfly.

WHEN do you add a new level? The rubric doesn't grow on any set schedule. But a good rule of thumb is to look to add one new level every 3-4 weeks.

That said, at the start of the year, new levels may be added more frequently, especially if your instruction begins with pictorial skills. Teaching students how to add details to their pictures tends to be easier for them and therefore, requires less practice time. Consequently, true-to-life colors, facial expressions, setting, background, and other close-up details are expectations that could be added to the growing rubric weekly.

Now, let me caution you: This rapid pace can feel overwhelming at first, as it might seem like you're heading toward a large number of levels by year's end. However, once students begin to write sentences, the frequency of adding levels to the rubric slows down. And since sentence writing comes with more to manage, like punctuation, capitalization, and sentence structure, they often require more practice before they can be added to the rubric. Consequently, students tend to linger in a level on the rubric longer, causing a slowdown in the rubric-updating lessons.

And while this is a reality, don't go too long before increasing the challenge. We don't want to lose out on the students' enthusiasm for self-assessment and writing improvement. If there aren't any new SKILLS you can add to your rubric, consider ways to increase the sophistication of current skills already listed. For example: Writing five sentences is good, but writing five sentences with varied sentence beginnings is even better. Writing complete thoughts with verbs is good, but choosing stronger action verbs is better. Connecting ideas with "so," "and," and "then" is good, but using "first," "next," and "also" is better. This ups the ante by requiring more than just a skill to be PRESENT in the writing. It increases the QUALITY of that skill's execution. This approach helps students see concrete ways to up their scores, keeping them motivated to continue to improve.

Honoring that there will be times in the year that levels increase frequently and longer stretches when it's only once a month, most primary teachers end the year with between 10-12 levels on their class writing rubric. (And don't forget, as writer expectations grow throughout the year, provide parents a copy of the rubric each time it is revised. They are another important stakeholder in the building of young writers.)

section_name: Never Remove Levels, Gradual Release, and Closing
content:
Episode 7, PK-2: Growing Rubrics — Never Remove Levels, Gradual Release, and Closing

I've spent a good portion of this video describing how to ADD levels, now let's address the notion of WHEN you remove levels. NEVER. Nope, not ever. Earlier I shared that the goal for each writer is to MOVE UP to the next level. We want to honor the journey these young writers have made; the hard work they did to move from L1, to L2 and L3. But, by removing a level, kids who WERE consistently writing 3-star products now find themselves back in level 2. That's definitely not motivating. Not to mention, I've had several primary teachers reflect that as they acquire NEW students mid-year, they often need the expectations at that lowest level, as students may not have had much writing instruction at their previous school.

We've learned that an instructional writing rubric reflects students' ongoing growth and evolves in tandem with your instruction. This thoughtful, gradual process meets students where they are and fosters continuous improvement for all learners.

As the year progresses, you will teach more writing skills that will eventually make their way onto the rubric criteria. And while you won't wait until all students have mastered the current skills before adding more, you also don't want to rush to add each skill immediately after introducing it. Rather, honor the gradual release of responsibility: INTRODUCE and model new skills in whole-class explicit instruction, AND then PROVIDE PLENTY of time for students to practice and apply them to their own independent writing. Students need ample time to internalize each new writing skill BEFORE being held accountable for it on the rubric.

For all these reasons, each classroom will develop its rubric at a different pace—even within the SAME grade level. While every class has both strong and emerging writers, the distribution of high and low skills may vary from class to class. We won't START with the same initial rubric, and we won't all GROW it in the same way. First-grade teachers will not have a single instructional rubric that works for all of their different classrooms.

Because the rubric is not a standardized data-collection tool, its content is tailored to meet the unique needs of each class. The pace at which new skills are added, and the criteria described, will reflect the developmental needs of the students in THAT specific classroom. This is where the instructional rubric becomes so valuable. With its evolving criteria, it helps students prioritize what they should focus on without overwhelming them with skills they aren't ready for.

That all said, it's crucial that the TEACHERS within the same grade level are hyper focused on their writing standards. While classroom rubrics in the different sections of first grade may not be identical THROUGHOUT the year, what's most important is that they all evolve toward the same end-of-year grade-level writing goals.

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaway. Building and growing a single writing rubric all year establishes a classroom culture that values effort and improvement. It's a way to make writing expectations clear, and foster self-reflection and revision.

So start with a simple rubric, raise the rigor as you teach more, and trust in your students' abilities to rise to the challenge. By empowering students with an assessment tool that they understand, we take the next step toward building better writers.
